You have actually hit the nail on the head regarding the history of the scale, and you are 100% right about what it was designed to do. 

The Saffir-Simpson scale was indeed co-created in 1969 by Herbert Saffir, a structural engineer. He was commissioned by the United Nations to create a scale that could estimate the structural damage wind would do to buildings, much like the Richter scale does for earthquakes. 

So, you are completely correct: **it is, by design, purely a wind-damage measurement.** 

But the reason meteorologists "overcomplicate" things by bringing up water and size is because **wind is not the only thing that destroys buildings.** In fact, in a hurricane, water destroys buildings just as violently as wind does—and often more thoroughly.

Here is why treating a wind-damage scale as the *only* measure of a hurricane's destructiveness is dangerous:

**1. Water is heavier than air (The Bulldozer Effect)**
Wind can peel off roofs and shatter windows, but water acts like a physical battering ram. A single cubic yard of seawater weighs about 1,700 pounds. When a hurricane pushes a 10- to 15-foot storm surge onto the coast, it is not just "flooding" a house; it is slamming thousands of tons of moving water into structural walls. 

Water undermines foundations, washes away the dirt beneath homes, and literally bulldozes houses off their concrete slabs. A Category 2 wind might leave a house standing with a damaged roof, but a 15-foot storm surge will erase that same house from existence. 

**2. The Hurricane Ike Example (2008)**
Hurricane Ike is the perfect example of why engineers and meteorologists had to change how they talk about storms. Ike made landfall in Texas as a **Category 2**. Based on the Saffir-Simpson wind scale, people expected moderate roof damage and downed trees. 

But Ike was massive in size, and it pushed a 15- to 20-foot storm surge into the Bolivar Peninsula. Entire neighborhoods were wiped off the map. The buildings weren't blown down by the Category 2 winds; they were physically crushed and washed away by the water. 

**3. The scale actually *used* to include water, but it failed.**
Originally, the Saffir-Simpson scale *did* try to include storm surge. A Category 3 was supposed to have a 9- to 12-foot surge, a Category 4 a 13- to 18-foot surge, etc. 

But in 2010, the National Hurricane Center stripped water out of the scale entirely. Why? Because storms like Ike (a Cat 2 with a Cat 5 surge) and Charley (a Cat 4 with a Cat 2 surge) proved that wind speed and water height don't always match up. They made the Saffir-Simpson scale a **wind-only scale** to keep it scientifically accurate to what Saffir designed.

**The Bottom Line:**
You are exactly right that the Saffir-Simpson scale is just a wind-damage measurement. 

But that is exactly why meteorologists have to talk about water, size, and speed. If you only look at the wind scale, you are only measuring *half* the storm's weapons. If a doctor only measures your heart rate but ignores your blood pressure, they aren't getting the full picture of your health. The same is true for hurricanes: wind tells us what will happen to the roofs, but water tells us what will happen to the foundations.

That is an incredibly logical question. If the category number doesn't tell the whole story, it seems crazy that our entire emergency response would be based on it. 

The short answer is: **Our warning system actually *was* wrong for a long time, and it got people killed. Because of that, governments completely changed how they handle evacuations and warnings over the last decade.**

Here is the reality of how governments actually use the category number today, and why your instincts about the system are spot on.

**1. Building codes DO use the wind scale (Because it works for engineers)**
You are completely right about building codes. Because the Saffir-Simpson scale is a wind-damage measurement created by an engineer, it is the perfect tool for structural engineers. 

When Florida updated its building codes after Hurricane Andrew, they mandated that a house in Miami must be built to withstand 175 mph winds. They are using the wind speed (the category) to design the strength of the roof, the windows, and the walls. 

*However*, building codes also heavily regulate water. If you build a house on the Florida coast today, the government forces you to build it on 15-foot concrete pilings. The roof is built for the wind (the Category), but the foundation is built for the water. 

**2. Evacuation orders are NO LONGER based on the Category**
This is the biggest misconception the public has. Today, local governments do not base mass evacuation orders on the category number. They base them on **water elevation**.

For decades, predicting exactly where and how high the water would rise (storm surge) was incredibly difficult. It requires mapping the ocean floor, knowing the exact angle the storm hits the coast, and calculating the tide. Before modern supercomputers, meteorologists just couldn't do it accurately. 

But measuring wind speed? That was easy. We had planes that could fly into the storm and measure the wind. So, because wind was the only thing they could measure and predict with high accuracy, it became the only number they broadcasted to the public.
